title: Meet the Farm Animals
cardDescription: Familiar farm animals, their young, and what covers or feeds them.
description: Spend a little time in the barnyard with an easy crossword about familiar farm animals, their young, and the words used to describe them.
focus: This puzzle brings together animal names and a few related barnyard words. Some clues ask for an adult animal, while others ask for its young or a group. The wording tells you which kind of name is needed.
solvingTip: Check whether the clue names a young animal, an adult, a body part, or a group. The same short word can have another meaning away from the farm. Use the animal named in the clue and any crossing letters to narrow it down.
words: Young animal born to a cow
Farm animal known for its woolly fleece
Young animal born to a ewe
Farm animal with a snout and a curly tail
Young animal born to a sow
Hoofed farm animal whose young is called a kid
Web-footed farm bird often heard quacking
Long-necked farm bird known for honking
Offspring of a male donkey and a female horse
Fiber shorn from a sheep's fleece
Hard covering at the end of a cow's foot
Dry grain stalks used as animal bedding

answerNotes.CALF: Calf is the young cattle animal here. The word can also name part of a human leg; the reference to a cow selects the animal meaning.
answerNotes.LAMB: A lamb is a young sheep. Ewe names an adult female, so the age and parent named in the clue matter.
answerNotes.KID: Kid has a specific animal meaning: a young goat. Its familiar use for a child is not the meaning requested here.
answerNotes.ROOSTER: Rooster is the usual American English name for an adult male chicken. A hen is the adult female.
answerNotes.HERD: Herd is used for cattle as a group. It sounds like heard, but the clue asks for a group name rather than something perceived by the ears.
answerNotes.FLOCK: Flock can name a group of sheep as well as a group of birds. The clue specifies the sheep meaning.
answerNotes.MULE: A mule has a male donkey and a female horse as parents. A hinny has the reverse parentage.
answerNotes.STRAW: Straw consists of dry stalks left from grain crops. Hay is dried forage, commonly grass or legumes; the two words describe different materials.

title: Across the Grain Fields
cardDescription: Grain crops, plant parts, and familiar fieldwork words.
description: Take a gentle trip across the fields with a crossword about grain crops, their plant parts, and familiar words for planting and harvesting.
focus: The clues move between crops, pieces of a plant, and work done in a field. An everyday word can take a particular meaning in farming. Each clue points to the intended object or action without requiring machinery specifications.
solvingTip: Notice whether the clue asks for something that grows, a part of that plant, a tool, or an action. Short crop names can provide useful crossing letters. Read the whole definition before choosing between two related fieldwork words.
words: Powered farm vehicle that can pull equipment
Farm implement that turns over soil before planting
Toothed farm implement used to break up soil clods
Long narrow trench made by a plow
Earth in which crop roots grow
Small plant structure sown to start a crop
Plants grown together for food or another useful product
Grain crop with kernels arranged on cobs
Grain commonly milled into flour for bread
Grain used to make traditional rolled breakfast cereal
Grain associated with dark bread and pumpernickel
Grain often served as small chewy pearls in soup
The harvested seeds of cereal crops, collectively
Main upright stem of a corn plant
Seed-bearing part of a corn plant, also a hearing organ
Fine threadlike strands at the tip of a corn cob
One grain on a corn cob
To put seeds into the ground for growing
To cut and gather a ripe grain crop
A straight line of planted crops

answerNotes.PLOW: Plow is the standard American spelling; plough is common in British English. Here it names the implement used to turn soil.
answerNotes.HARROW: A harrow works the soil with teeth or discs, breaking clods or smoothing the surface. A plow and a harrow have related but different jobs.
answerNotes.FURROW: Furrow names a narrow trench in the soil. It can also describe a crease in a brow, but the plow fixes the field meaning.
answerNotes.EAR: An ear of corn is the seed-bearing structure on the plant. The word is shared with the body part, which makes the crop context useful.
answerNotes.SILK: Corn silk is the cluster of fine strands associated with an ear of corn. In this clue, silk refers to those plant strands rather than woven fabric.
answerNotes.KERNEL: A kernel is an individual grain, such as one on a corn cob. The cob supports many kernels; it is not itself a single kernel.
answerNotes.SOW: Sow means plant seeds here and rhymes with go. The word for an adult female pig has the same spelling but a different pronunciation.
answerNotes.REAP: Reap means cut and gather a crop. Sowing begins a growing season, while reaping belongs to the harvest.

title: A Visit to the Orchard
cardDescription: Fruit names, tree parts, and a few orchard harvest words.
description: Visit the orchard through a crossword about familiar tree fruits, the parts of a fruit tree, and everyday harvest words.
focus: This puzzle looks at fruit from the tree to the picking basket. Clues distinguish tree parts from fruit parts and describe familiar fruits by a characteristic feature. No knowledge of named cultivars or growing zones is needed.
solvingTip: Use the clue to decide whether the answer is a fruit, part of a tree, part of the fruit, or something used at harvest. A single large stone and a central seed-bearing section have different names. Crossing letters can help separate similar fruit names.
words: An area planted with fruit trees
Tree fruit often pressed into cider
Fruit whose familiar shape is narrow at the top and wider below
Fuzzy-skinned fruit with a large stone inside
Smooth-skinned stone fruit often purple in color
Small round stone fruit often sold with its slender stem
Small orange-colored stone fruit often dried
Seed-bearing produce such as apples and peaches
Woody limb extending from a tree's main stem
Main woody stem of a tree
Underground plant part that absorbs water
A flower on a fruit tree
Small unopened growth that may become a leaf or flower
Central seed-bearing section of an apple
Outer skin removed from a piece of fruit
Ready to eat or harvest, as mature fruit
To pluck fruit from a tree
Equipment with rungs used to reach high branches
Woven container used for gathering fruit

answerNotes.ORCHARD: An orchard is land planted with fruit or nut trees. In this puzzle the clues focus on fruit trees rather than nut crops.
answerNotes.PEACH: A peach commonly has fuzzy skin and a large inner stone. Nectarines are closely related fruits with smooth skin.
answerNotes.APRICOT: Apricots are stone fruits, like peaches and plums. The clue uses their familiar small size, orange color, and dried form.
answerNotes.TRUNK: Trunk means the main woody stem here. The fruit-tree setting distinguishes it from a car storage compartment or a large travel chest.
answerNotes.BLOSSOM: Blossom names a flower, especially one on a fruit tree. The flower and the later fruit are different stages of development.
answerNotes.PIT: Pit is the usual American word for the hard stone inside a peach. It differs from the softer central core of an apple.
answerNotes.CORE: An apple core is the central section containing the seeds. It is not the same structure as the single hard pit of a peach.
answerNotes.RIPE: Ripe describes fruit that has reached a suitable stage for eating or harvest. The clue asks for a condition rather than a particular fruit.

title: Around the Horse Stable
cardDescription: Horse names, riding equipment, and stable vocabulary.
description: Step into the stable with an easy crossword about horses, riding equipment, and the familiar words used in their daily care.
focus: The answers include names for horses, items of riding equipment, and words for movement and stable surroundings. The clues describe what an item does or where it goes, so a rider's technical background is not required.
solvingTip: Watch for clues about a type of horse, equipment, movement, or a body part. Headgear used to guide a horse and a support for a rider's foot serve different purposes. Let the described job and the crossing letters help with longer equipment names.
words: Large hoofed animal commonly ridden with a saddle
A horse of a small type, rather than simply a young one
A young horse of either sex
An adult male horse that has not been gelded
Rider's seat fastened on a horse's back
Headgear used to guide a horse when riding
Straps a rider holds to guide a horse
Headgear used to lead or tie a horse
Hanging foot support on a riding saddle
To brush and clean a horse's coat
Bristled tool used to clean a horse's coat
Long hair along a horse's neck
Horse's rear appendage that can swish away flies
A horse's two-beat gait, faster than a walk
Fast four-beat running gait of a horse
Individual compartment for a horse in a stable
Dried grass or other forage fed to horses
Hard outer covering of a horse's foot

answerNotes.PONY: Pony describes a small type of horse, not a horse's age. A foal is a young horse and may grow into a large adult.
answerNotes.FOAL: Foal can refer to a young horse of either sex. Colt and filly are more specific names for a young male and young female.
answerNotes.MARE: Mare names an adult female horse. The clue asks for the adult rather than the young female, called a filly.
answerNotes.BRIDLE: A bridle is riding headgear used to help guide a horse. A halter is generally used for leading or tying, so the purpose distinguishes the items.
answerNotes.REINS: Reins are straps held by the rider. Rein, rain, and reign sound alike in ordinary American pronunciation, but have different spellings and meanings.
answerNotes.HALTER: A halter is headgear for leading or tying a horse. The clue describes that handling purpose rather than the rider's seat or foot support.
answerNotes.STIRRUP: A stirrup supports a rider's foot and hangs from the saddle. Its position distinguishes it from the reins held in the hands.
answerNotes.TROT: The trot is a two-beat gait. The walk and gallop have different footfall patterns, so the beat count helps identify the movement.
answerNotes.HAY: Hay is dried forage used as animal feed. Straw is made from dry grain stalks and is commonly used as bedding.

title: At the Country Fair
cardDescription: Rural fair exhibits, homemade entries, and judging words.
description: Enjoy a visit to a country fair through familiar words for exhibits, homemade entries, and the ribbons awarded after judging.
focus: This puzzle focuses on the display side of a rural fair: things people enter, places they show them, and words used in judging. A fair may include many other activities, but these clues stay with familiar exhibits and prizes.
solvingTip: Ask whether a clue describes an entered item, a display place, a person, or an award. Some everyday words change meaning in a competition. Color clues specify the United States convention to help identify a prize ribbon.
words: Community event with exhibits, contests, and entertainment
An item or collection put on public view
Narrow fabric award given after judging
Person who evaluates entries in a competition
Award given to a winning entry
Small stand used by a seller or exhibitor
Enclosed area used for a livestock show
Organized procession of people or decorated vehicles
Layered stitched bedcover entered in a needlework display
Fruit preserve that might be entered in a canning contest
Baked dish with pastry and a sweet or savory filling
Sweet baked dessert often entered in a decorating contest
An activity that makes decorative objects by hand
An item submitted for a competition
An arrangement of objects put out for people to see
An event where animals or other entries are presented
Person or entry awarded first place
Traditional first-place ribbon color at many U.S. fairs
Traditional second-place ribbon color at many U.S. fairs

answerNotes.EXHIBIT: Exhibit is used as a noun here for something put on public view. As a verb it can mean to display that item.
answerNotes.RIBBON: A ribbon is a fabric award in this setting. Its color may communicate a placing or judging result, depending on the fair's system.
answerNotes.JUDGE: Judge names the person evaluating entries here. The same word can be a verb meaning to evaluate, so the wording asking for a person matters.
answerNotes.BOOTH: A booth is a small stand or space for a seller or exhibitor. It need not be a fully enclosed room.
answerNotes.QUILT: A quilt has layers joined by stitching. It can be displayed and judged for needlework rather than entered as a food or livestock exhibit.
answerNotes.JAM: Jam is the fruit preserve in this clue. A traffic jam is an unrelated use of the same short word.
answerNotes.ENTRY: Entry names an item submitted to a contest. It does not mean a doorway or the act of arriving in this clue.
answerNotes.BLUE: Blue is traditionally associated with first place at many U.S. fairs. Individual fairs and judging systems can use ribbons differently.
answerNotes.RED: Red often indicates second place in a U.S. placing system. The clue specifies that convention; ribbon colors are not universal.
